title: The Civic Role of the Tech Elite
author: Aaron Renn
summary: Aaron Renn's digest addresses three distinct but related themes: the civic obligations of the tech elite in an era of concentrated wealth; the failure of conservative institutions to maintain public goods like libraries; and the personal challenge of holding individual standards in a post-sexual-revolution environment where the behaviors those standards once excluded are now socially normalized. The civic-obligation section centers on a contrast between the tech elite's new political visibility and the older model of civic philanthropy represented by the Simon brothers, who purchased the Indiana Pacers not primarily as an investment but as a duty to Indianapolis -- an act Renn argues was consciously understood as a bad financial deal undertaken because powerful people have obligations to the cities that made their success possible. Renn contrasts this with a pattern of tech-wealth civic engagement that is geographically unrooted, algorithmically distributed, and optimized for influence rather than local stewardship. The library section argues that conservatives have ceded an important civic institution to progressive capture not because they lost a political fight but because they neglected an institution they depended on others to maintain. The personal standards section is the most personal: Renn reflects on the difficulty of maintaining pre-sexual-revolution behavioral expectations in an environment where most peers, including most religious peers, have de facto abandoned them, and where holding those standards increasingly means navigating relationships with people for whom your standards would constitute a judgment on their choices.
points: The Simon brothers' purchase of the Indiana Pacers is the model of tech-elite civic obligation Renn invokes: a deliberate bad investment made because powerful people owe something to the communities that built them.

Tech-wealth civic engagement is geographically unrooted and algorithmically distributed -- optimized for influence reach rather than the local stewardship that characterized mid-century industrial philanthropy.
Conservative institutional neglect of libraries is not defeat in a culture war; it is the failure to steward a civic institution that requires active maintenance, not passive non-interference.

Holding personal behavioral standards in a post-sexual-revolution environment is increasingly difficult not because the standards have changed but because the social context that made them normal has dissolved.

The hardest form of personal integrity is holding a standard whose violation by others you must navigate without performing judgment -- maintaining the practice without making it a verdict on everyone around you.
quotes: The Simon brothers bought the Pacers because Indianapolis needed someone to. That is a form of civic reasoning that has largely disappeared from the elite class. They knew it was a bad investment. They did it anyway, because powerful people have obligations to the places that made them powerful.

Tech-wealth philanthropy is geographically unmoored in a way that mid-century industrial philanthropy was not. The Carnegie library was in Pittsburgh because Carnegie was from Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh made Carnegie. The algorithm does not make that kind of demand.

Conservatives did not lose the libraries in a fight. They ceded them through neglect -- the assumption that institutions they valued but did not tend would remain as they found them. That is not how institutions work.

The difficulty of holding pre-revolution behavioral standards today is not primarily external. It is internal: you are holding a standard that your own community has largely abandoned, and doing so without the social reinforcement that made those standards sustainable for previous generations.

The question is not whether your standards are right. The question is whether you can hold them without converting every relationship with someone who lives differently into a referendum on their choices. That is actually quite hard.
